messages:
noah: Quick follow-up to the RFC thread024: should we separate service-level authz from org/project scoping?
elaine: tl;dr: decoupling makes service policies simpler but we must ensure tenant isolation doesn't degrade.
ravi: If we decouple, we need a binding contract: which projects can a service act on? Without that, we open lateral access.
maya: Two main approaches I see: 1) central broker that mints project-scoped ephemeral tokens 2) attribute-based tokens validated at runtime with policy checks.
noah: Broker tradeoffs?
maya: Pros: auditable mint events, easy revocation per project, explicit lineage. Cons: an extra network hop, state + HA burden, migration cost.
elaine: Attr-based tokens pros: stateless runtime, fewer moving pieces. Cons: must be strongly signed and audience-checked; harder to constrain and prove intent later.
ravi: Important detail: any token used across projects must include both: originating service_id and target project_id as claims. No wildcards.
ops-bot: Deploy note: introducing a broker touches token-issuer, authz-api, and operator runbooks. Recommend canary rollout in staging with 2 low-risk services.
noah: Migration plan idea: broker optional initially. Services can keep legacy keys; they call broker for cross-project calls when needed. Introduce header X-Authz-Mode: legacy|scoped|required.
maya: Example mint flow:
```
POST /broker/mint
{ "service_id": "svc-ingest", "project_id": "proj-123", "purpose": "write" }
-> { "scoped_token": "ey...", "expires_at": "2026-06-01T12:00:00Z" }
```
Service uses scoped_token for downstream request. Tokens = audience-bound, signed, include jti, service_id, project_id, exp.
elaine: Observability: broker must emit mint events with mint_reason and caller context so we can answer "which service/project triggered this action". Also surface mint latency and cache hit rates.
ravi: Performance: minting adds latency once per TTL. Cache scoped tokens in-service for short TTLs to amortize. For high fanout jobs, prefer issuing per-project tokens in batch or provide an ephemeral worker with elevated project ACL and stronger audit.
noah: Security checks: rotation UX for broker keys, SLOs for broker availability, replay protection via jti+nonce, short token TTLs.
m a ya: (typo) maya: Also consider a mint_rate limit per service/project to prevent amplification.
elaine: Policy model point: preserve existing project-level RBAC (roles bound to project resources) and add optional service-scoped bindings rather than invent a new role grammar. Keep policy evaluation semantics familiar.
noah: Edge-case: background jobs that touch thousands of projects. Do not mint thousands of tokens synchronously. Options: 1) batch mint endpoint 2) ephemeral worker with explicit elevated ACL + tight audit 3) designate a limited set of service accounts for bulk ops.
ravi: Rollout milestones suggestion:
1) design + security review
2) broker prototype + SDK helper + basic metrics
3) internal canary with 2 non-critical services
4) opt-in rollout using X-Authz-Mode header + telemetry
5) require scoped tokens for selected cross-project endpoints
6) deprecate legacy long-lived cross-project keys
maya: Dev UX: provide SDK helpers that transparently mint + cache tokens and fall back to legacy key with a loud warning. Also provide CLI for operators to mint tokens for manual debugging.
ops-bot: Ops checklist: broker HA (multi-AZ), mint_rate and error metrics, latency SLO, runbook for broker outage and revoke procedures.
elaine: Incident playbook sketch: broker outage -> detect increased legacy-key usage -> enforce temporary read-only cross-project policy -> expedite rotation or scale broker -> post-incident audit of minted tokens and any elevated access.
noah: Questions for the RFC follow-up doc: what endpoints will require scoped tokens first? How long should default TTL be? What is acceptable broker SLO?
ravi: Propose defaults: TTL 5m for high-sensitivity write ops, 15-60m for read-only caches. Broker SLO 99.9 for mint success; design to degrade gracefully (clear fallback path).
maya: I'll prototype the SDK helper + cache logic. Ravi can prototype the mint endpoint. Elaine can update policy model notes. Noah will draft the RFC addendum and timeline.
noah: Great. I'll include these milestones, ops checklist, security notes, and an opt-in header plan in the follow-up RFC. Tagging this for the next auth sync. :thumbsup:
